sections.h2: Where to record a deed in Scioto County
sections.html:
Deeds for Scioto County land are recorded at the Scioto County Recorder's Office, 602 7th St., Room 110, Portsmouth, Ohio 45662. Counter service starts at 8:00 am on weekdays and stops at 4:00 pm; the line is (740) 355-8304. Portsmouth is the county seat, and the auditor and treasurer have offices at that same 7th Street address.

You can file in person or by mail. Mail filers should enclose a self-addressed stamped envelope. Without one, the office charges postage to send the original back.

sections.h2: Paying the recorder and formatting the document
sections.html:
The recorder takes cash or a check, and nothing else. Make the check payable to "Scioto County Recorder", because checks written to a second or third party are refused. Scioto County has also adopted the $5.00 record preservation fee on top of its other recording charges.

A deed must meet these layout rules before it will be accepted:

  • Legible type of size ten or larger, in blue or black ink only
  • Letter or legal size sheets (8 1/2 by 11, or 8 1/2 by 14)
  • No highlighted text
  • One inch margins at the sides and bottom
  • Three blank inches above the text on page one, and an inch and a half above it on every later page

A deed that misses these rules can be turned away, which delays your closing. Have the attorney or title agency preparing the deed check them before signing.

The recorder's checklist reads like this: write the deed on a fresh form rather than copying the old one, borrow the legal description from the last recorded deed, have a notary witness the signing, take the transfer to the Scioto County Auditor, and bring the deed back to the recorder once that office is done.

The auditor bills a transfer charge of its own, apart from the recorder's. That counter is Room 103 (740.355.8264) and stays open until 4:30 pm.

Two related points matter to sellers. After a payoff, the lender files a release of mortgage as its own document, and no new deed appears. And mobile home titles are not kept at the recorder, because they are registered with the county auditor.

The auditor's transfer charges come from R.C. 319.54(G), and Chapter 322 allows an added county transfer tax. The county's full recording fee list is a separate sheet, so request it from the recorder before sending payment.

Auditor fees under R.C. 319.54(G)
Auditor serviceFee
Transfer or entry of a lot or parcel of landFifty cents for each transfer or entry, paid by the person requiring it
Receiving the statement of value (conveyance fee)One dollar, or ten cents for each one hundred dollars or fraction, whichever is greater
Deed of land sold for taxesFive dollars, paid by the purchaser

Section 319.54(G)(3) excuses certain deeds from the conveyance fee: those given only as security for a debt, corrective deeds, and no-money transfers between heirs are examples. An excused deed travels with a short statement of the reason.

sections.h2: What the Recorder cannot do for you
sections.html:
The office does not draft documents or offer legal advice. A fill-in-the-blank form still requires choices that count as legal advice.

  • It cannot tell you whether you hold good and clear title. Title examiners search the recorder's index and other county offices to decide that.
  • It does not remove or release liens. A federal tax lien is recorded there, but only the issuing agency can release it.
  • Searching is left to you or a title professional, even though the records are public.
  • Birth and death certificates come from the county health department, and divorce and marriage records come from the clerk of courts and probate court.

Let the title company run the lien search. Property tax liens are the treasurer's business, so raise those with that office.

Beyond deeds, the office records mortgages, mortgage releases, plats and financing statements under the Uniform Commercial Code that relate to real estate. Surveys are not usually filed there, so ask your lender or title company for one. If your home is in a subdivision, a plat map can be found by searching the subdivision name, and it shows lot lines and streets without any buildings.

Certified copies carry the office's stamp, so a printout from home cannot be certified. Come to the counter or request them by mail with a self-addressed stamped envelope. A document that cites an earlier recorded one through a marginal notation costs an extra charge per reference.

sections.h2: Searching records and guarding against deed fraud
sections.html:
The recorder's website offers a public records search and, as a trial, a newer mobile-friendly portal that opens recorded documents on a phone. Parcels can also be found on a GIS map kept by the county engineer, searchable by owner name, address or parcel number.

The site also offers Property Fraud Alert, a free service that monitors your name and flags new filings. It cannot block fraud, so treat it as an early warning. Notaries get a similar free service that watches for their name or commission number.

Scioto County has an estimated 71,365 residents, 33,078 housing units and 28,864 households. Owners occupy 68.4 percent of homes, and the typical owner-occupied home is valued at $137,900. Median gross rent is $742. Portsmouth is the only city, with New Boston, Otway, Rarden and South Webster as villages. Much of the western half is forest, so acreage sales are common.

sections.h2: Property tax dates and your sale
sections.html:
State law splits the annual real estate bill into two installments, the later one falling on June 20 unless extended. The county moved the later installment in 2026 because of House Bill 186, so read the date printed on your bill. Your closing agent requests a tax payoff from the treasurer, whose office is at 602 7th Street, Room 102.

For assessment dates, appeals and relief programs, see the Scioto County property tax guide on this site.

On closing day the order is the same for a cash sale or a financed one: the notary witnesses your signature, the title company holds back the tax payoff, the auditor endorses the deed, and the recorder records it. If a lender is paid off, the release of mortgage is filed separately.

Ask the title company for a certified copy of the recorded deed once it is done. It carries the office's stamp and works for later loans or sales, and it is the only form of copy that counts as official.

faqs.q: When can I visit the Scioto County Recorder?
faqs.a: Weekdays from 8:00 am, with the last service at 4:00 pm, in Room 110 at 602 7th St., Portsmouth. Call (740) 355-8304 to check.

faqs.q: How do I pay to record a deed in Scioto County?
faqs.a: Pay by cash or by a check made out to "Scioto County Recorder". Checks payable to anyone else are refused. The county has also adopted a $5.00 record preservation fee.

faqs.q: Is a notary required on a Scioto County deed?
faqs.a: Yes. Every transfer is signed before a notary. Ohio law also allows a judge, a clerk of court, the county auditor, the county engineer or a mayor to take the acknowledgment.

faqs.q: Does the recorder issue a new deed when I pay off my mortgage?
faqs.a: No. A new deed is issued only when the property is transferred. When the loan is satisfied, your lender files a release of mortgage as a separate recorded document.

faqs.q: Can the recorder tell me whether my title is clear?
faqs.a: No. The office is not allowed to give opinions on title. A professional title examiner or abstractor reviews the recorder's index along with records at other county offices.
